{"title":"Spatial & Interaction Patterns: exp-E-decision Evacuation","narrative":"The evacuation took place in a 38×38 cell interior with a single 3-cell wide exit door located at x=39, y=18–20. Throughout the run, all 100 person agents moved eastward toward this aperture at a fixed speed of 1.0 cell/step, resulting in a clear funneling of movement lines converging on the door region.

As agents approached the door, the block-on-collision rule caused them to slow and accumulate, generating a high-density cluster immediately upstream of the exit. This queue extended back into the room as more agents joined the bottleneck, with no significant off-path aggregations observed elsewhere in the space.

There was no evidence of territorial segregation or persistent sub-group clustering away from the exit: initial positions dispersed uniformly and all interactions centered on the doorway. Once an agent passed through the door (x=39, y=18–20), it was removed, steadily reducing the local density until the queue dissolved.

The spatial structure shaped the outcome by creating a self-organized queuing pattern at the bottleneck. Despite the randomized seed driving initial placement, the single narrow door reliably produced a dense, temporary jam that only cleared as agents exited in turn.","key_findings":["All 100 agents converged on the single exit at x=39, y=18–20, producing a focused flow.","Collision blocking led to a persistent high-density cluster directly in front of the 3-cell door.","No secondary clusters or territorial zones formed elsewhere in the room.","Exit throughput increased only after the queue thinned, showing a classic bottleneck effect.","Agents evacuated completely before the 300-step cap, demonstrating eventual decongestion."],"causal_links":["Block-on-collision rule → formation of dense agent cluster at door","Narrow 3-cell door width → bottleneck and queuing behavior"],"emergent_phenomena":["Self-organized single-file queue at the exit","System-level bottleneck flow not specified by any individual rule but arising from spatial constraints and collision interactions"]}
